story_text.value:
Recently, I've been reading a bunch of books trying to disprove my own belief that AI trading bots won't eventually take away all the edge in the market and leave no opportunities behind. I've always disagreed with the Efficient Market Hypothesis, much like Edward Thorp.

In one of the books I read,(The Migration of Scarcity)

A weather forecast does not change the weather, Edrin. A market forecast is part of the weather.

A forecast in such a market does not describe a state that exists independently of it. It selects among states, each of which would make it true. Forecasting becomes coordination.

I guess if I had to put the thing that made me disagree with the theory into words, this would be it.

title.value: Is AI going to arb away all market inefficiencies?

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I have been working on mxRaven: https://mxraven.com for the past couple of months, and it has been hard to explain the idea without actually showcasing a functional use case, hence I decided to build perch.

Perch is a single binary Go program that can serve IMAP + SMTP as a complete mailbox service and has an agent-friendly CLI to access and manage emails.

Note that perch is open source under the MIT-0 license but it requires mxRaven to handle the public edge. However, the CLI (the `perch mail` command) can be used against any generic IMAP or SMTP submission servers (which are not necessarily perch). You can try out perch without signing up for mxRaven at https://tryperch.mxraven.com and can sign up for a free account with monthly 1k inbound + 1k outbound emails without a card.

The agent-friendly CLI was not an afterthought, since LLMs have been trained heavily for utilizing POSIX-compatible shell tools for various benchmarks, I believe agents are unbelievably good when you give them tools in the language they understand: CLI.

Perch can run on an old workstation in your homelab behind CGNAT or firewalls as it pulls mail in real-time from mxRaven's notification stream over a websocket. It also doesn't need to run 24*7, it can come online atleast once a day to pull the emails from mxRaven. mxRaven will not retain emails that are older than 48 hours as per our privacy policy, and it will not serve them to the pull-based consumer beyond 24 hours.

The hardest part about self-hosting email is the public edge, which requires managing IP reputation, throttles and a convoluted set of authentication protocols (DKIM, SPF, DMARC, ARC etc.) and mxRaven handles that.

Note that we also made a Show HN post for mxRaven itself here: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50338055

tldr, for those who don't want to read that: think of mxRaven as the WAF + router for your emails, while your applications can sit on the driver's seat for the email highway.

story_text.value:
hi HN!

I built Mimzie, an agent neutral AI workspace inspired by the Claude Suite (Docs, Sheets, Slides) and Cowork.

It's a free desktop app that runs ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Grok in their native CLI harnesses. Think T3 Code or Conductor but for knowledge work. It's basically a GUI for managing knowledge work agents in various form factors. One of those form factors is Bots, akin to Grok Bot or Dots.

The original idea for mimzie was simple: I pay for Claude and ChatGPT, and a lot of my day-to-day work lives in .xlsx, .pptx and .docx files. Moreover, I was sick and tired of losing context between AI platforms. I didn't want to bet the house on one AI lab's product, be it the ChatGPT or the Claude Desktop app.

So I built an AI desktop app that was agent neutral.

The goal of mimzie is to bring the kind of agent workflows that devs have had with codex and claude code into the hands of everyone. And to have a friendly GUI to do it. I've found that the personal agents, hermes and openclaw, are intimidating to set up and confusing to the average non-technical person.

some of the core principles of mimzie:

- your file stays your file: edits are done locally and .docx, .pptx, .xlsx, and .md and synced to the cloud after - every change is reviewable: edits show up as tracked diffs that you accept or reject, at the smallest unit that makes sense (e.g. a sentence in .docx) - free, and no new subscription needed: bring whichever AI plan or plans you already have. You shouldn't have to pay twice for the same inference, and you SHOULD take advantage of the insane subsidization in the current ChatGPT and Claude plans. - Bots with any AI: I love the concept of grok bot, not so much its limited choice of models. I strongly believe that long-standing "ai teammates" should be agent neutral and in your control

Try mimzie out: it's a free beta at mimzie.com

it's early, lots of rough edges, but I've had the time of my life developing it.

I'd love to answer questions and hear any and all feedback.

story_text.value: I had been staring at some of the empty walls in my home and wanted to put up some frames but was always worried about the right measurements on where to put the holes, you can enter the size of the wall and the frames that you already have or planning to buy, or pick from your iphone gallery(photo library is used to show your artwork inside a frame) choose the layout and it will tell where you need to drill the holes measured from the floor and left edge of the wall, see the frames on your real wall with AR. The math accounts for wires drop, d-rings which need two nails at the same height. Built in SwiftUI. I have used RealityKit for the AR preview. The math turned out to be a bit trickier than I had thought. A frame usually doesn’t hang from its top edge since wire pulls up into a point below the top and D-rings need two nails at the same height and if you measure each frame from the one next to it then small errors add up. So had to account for measuring every nail from the floor and the same wall corner.

story_text.value:
I'm having a really hard time working with claude. In the past when I wrote all the code manually, it was always carefully reviewed and architected, with all possible flows carefully mapped out. Now, my code is mostly AI written which has led to things going out of control. Since it's easy to add new features and support many user flows, we went ahead and implemented flows that support a lot of cases our users run into. But now, I feel like things are getting too complex with no central notion of behaviour definitions, which causes every bug-fixing session to feel like a game of whack-a-mole, and results in missing edge cases and UI bugs that are becoming impossible to review and keep track of.

Every time I build anything new, it adds more complexity and the agent only seems to focus on the surrounding code within that session without keeping track of how it fits into the rest of the code base/product.

How do you all deal with this? Any suggestions for improving?

title.value: How do you keep up quality when you vibe-code?

story_text.value:
Browsers natively handle a lot of what used to take 50 lines of JS (or a dependency): `CSS.highlights` for text range highlighting without <span>s everywhere, `<dialog>` and showModal() give you backdrops and ideal focus management, `field-sizing` to auto-grow textareas as the user types.. (Something yesterday's ftrain post touched on [0])

Models know about some of these by name, but consistently won't default to using the platform-native solution and instead prefer the incumbent <div>+JS based pattern. We started an effort in Chrome to supplement coding agents with this key domain knowledge and we're shipping our 1.0 today, in collaboration with Firefox, MDN, and Edge.

200+ guides (~1.7MB) of curated, hand-crafted implementation best-practices from web experts, updated as the web evolves. (Open source, obv, so.. we'll welcome your bikeshedding ;) Readable versions here: [1]

I've spent the last 9 months obsessing over how to ship this as an agent skill + (Agentic RAG) CLI without blowing up your context window. (Or cedeing activation mechanics to MCP dynamic tool search). The skill description is minmaxed for activating on relevant frontend tasks. The RAG work I'm pretty proud of… originally a 500mb native stack down to a ~7MB pure-JS package, ~10ms search on your CPU.

We just introduced a deterministic 'legacy-scan' (trained on 30k github repos) to identify old 'n dusted patterns that your agent can modernize. (92% avg precision on held-out repos.)

People make a lot of claims about what coding agents are good/bad at. We wanted receipts, so we invested heavily in eval infra [2] to help us hill-climb, but also to identify when knowledge is common enough we can prune our guides. (Ofc, some of the things we thought AI didn't know turned out to be wrong :) We run codex/claude/agy against 200 tasks without the skill and then with.. In total ~1,700 playwright/AST-based assertions. Agents go from 55% pass unguided to 92% guided.

Try it out:

    DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 npx modern-web-guidance@latest install
    DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 npx modern-web-guidance@latest search "animate dialog modal"
    DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 npx modern-web-guidance@latest legacy-scan ./src
If you spot something wrong or weird, give us a holler!

Longer write-up on the 1.0: https://developer.chrome.com/blog/modern-web-guidance-v1

1: https://developer.chrome.com/docs/modern-web-guidance/guides

2: https://googlechrome.github.io/modern-web-guidance-src/

story_text.value:
Annoyed by slow zip handling in Ruby apps in gems like roo and caxlsx, they use rubyzip underneath which is pure Ruby and does a lot of per entry work in Ruby objects which is slow.

My project keeps the rubyzip API (Zip::File, Zip::InputStream, etc.) but does the parsing compression and file IO in Rust, using the zip crate via magnus/rb-sys. Change a line in your gemfile and I ship precompiled gems so no Rust toolchain to install.

About 6x faster reading lots of small entries, and 2x faster deflating big ones. It also adds a few things rubyzip doesn’t have like limits for zip bombs, an open mode that doesn’t modify the archive, and multithreaded compression.

To check I didn’t break anything, I run rubyzip’s own test suite against it (416 of 476 pass; most of the rest test rubyzip internals), fuzz it against Python’s zipfile, and run the test suites of roo, caxlsx, rubyXL and a few others with ziperu swapped in, working pretty well so far.

I would love to hear ideas for new features, or zip edge cases that annoy you!

title.value: Show HN: Ziperu is rubyzip with a Rust core, same API but faster and safer

story_text.value:
Hi HN! I'm Claudia, first employee and founding researcher at Nuance Labs. We're a research startup based in Seattle and have just released what we've been working on for the past 18 months.

Emma, a conversational audio-visual AI that you can have a video call with in real time. It might be a little rough around the edges but we think it's better than anything else out there (we're biased, of course). You don't need to make an account and it works from the browser with mic and optionally camera.

Emma is built on our full-duplex audio-visual system, Nuplex. We focused on naturalness over existing benchmarks as we found they didn't correlate well with what people actually like or how we speak face to face. We think being uniquely expressive is more important than an averaged-out face, for example. Our blog goes into more detail: https://research.nuancelabs.ai/

A beta developer API is available at https://platform.nuancelabs.ai/. We're taking safety very seriously so she may prematurely end the call, in particular for the API, but we're working on tuning that.

Personality, across all modalities, was the most important part for me. I've spent the longest speaking to her and I think she can be a lot of fun! I'd love for people to try it out and I look forward to hearing what you all think.

Thank you!

(Apologies for the double post, someone external posted our demo before we were ready, oops: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50429477)

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm Noah. Negs runs spektrafilm, Andrea Volpato's physically based film simulation, in your browser (it's completely rewritten in Rust and using WebGPU). Drop in a photo (JPEG, PNG, TIFF or a RAW), pick a film and a print paper, and drag the sliders. The picture updates as you drag, and nothing is uploaded: it all runs on your machine.

Try it: https://getnegs.com/try/

Code (GPLv3): https://github.com/noahhaasis/negs

There are also native apps on the same engine: SwiftUI on macOS, GTK4 on Linux, and Windows.

Spektrafilm (it started life as agx-emulsion) isn't a LUT or a preset. It simulates the whole analog chain, negative and then print, using only the manufacturers' published datasheets. Andrea's original write-up on discuss.pixls.us is worth reading in full: https://discuss.pixls.us/t/spectral-film-simulations-from-sc.... Roughly, it goes like this:

- Your RGB image is turned back into a light spectrum and exposed onto the film's three dye layers through their published spectral sensitivity curves. - Each layer builds up density along its characteristic curve. Datasheet curves are measured with densitometers that see all three dyes at once, so they're first separated into a curve for each layer. - DIR couplers: where one layer develops a lot of density, it releases inhibitors that hold back development nearby, in the same layer and the ones next to it. This is where film's saturation and its edge sharpness come from. - Grain is simulated per layer, with fast and slow sub-layers, as random silver halide particles that become dye clouds. It depends on the density at each spot instead of being laid over the image. - Halation: light passes through the emulsion, bounces off the film base and exposes the red layer again (it's at the back), which gives the red glow around highlights. - The negative's dye spectra are then projected through a virtual enlarger with Y/M filtration onto print paper, which has its own sensitivities and curves, and the print is scanned back to RGB.

Because it's a model, the controls are physical: camera exposure, print exposure, enlarger filters, how much DIR coupling, grain particle size, halation strength. Push them too far and the image breaks the way film does, with colour crossovers when it's badly over- or underexposed. And you can experimentw with each control. There are about 50 stocks: Portra, Ektar, Gold, Pro 400H, Superia, Kodachrome, Velvia and Provia slide film, Aerochrome and some B&W (HP5, FP4...). There are 9 papers and print films too, such as Endura, Crystal Archive and Vision 2383. The paper choice has a huge impact on the final look.

Negs implements the entire chain and is orders of magnitudes faster than the original python Spektrafilm implementation, so you can play around with sliders and get live feedback.

Feedback is very welcome, especially from people who have actually shot these stocks: tell me which ones look wrong to you.

title.value: Show HN: Negs (Spektrafilm) brings spectral film simulations to the browser

hits.author: haasisnoah
hits.story_text:
Hi HN, I'm Noah. Negs runs spektrafilm, Andrea Volpato's physically based film simulation, in your browser (it's completely rewritten in Rust and using WebGPU). Drop in a photo (JPEG, PNG, TIFF or a RAW), pick a film and a print paper, and drag the sliders. The picture updates as you drag, and nothing is uploaded: it all runs on your machine.

Try it: https://getnegs.com/try/

Code (GPLv3): https://github.com/noahhaasis/negs

There are also native apps on the same engine: SwiftUI on macOS, GTK4 on Linux, and Windows.

Spektrafilm (it started life as agx-emulsion) isn't a LUT or a preset. It simulates the whole analog chain, negative and then print, using only the manufacturers' published datasheets. Andrea's original write-up on discuss.pixls.us is worth reading in full: https://discuss.pixls.us/t/spectral-film-simulations-from-sc.... Roughly, it goes like this:

- Your RGB image is turned back into a light spectrum and exposed onto the film's three dye layers through their published spectral sensitivity curves. - Each layer builds up density along its characteristic curve. Datasheet curves are measured with densitometers that see all three dyes at once, so they're first separated into a curve for each layer. - DIR couplers: where one layer develops a lot of density, it releases inhibitors that hold back development nearby, in the same layer and the ones next to it. This is where film's saturation and its edge sharpness come from. - Grain is simulated per layer, with fast and slow sub-layers, as random silver halide particles that become dye clouds. It depends on the density at each spot instead of being laid over the image. - Halation: light passes through the emulsion, bounces off the film base and exposes the red layer again (it's at the back), which gives the red glow around highlights. - The negative's dye spectra are then projected through a virtual enlarger with Y/M filtration onto print paper, which has its own sensitivities and curves, and the print is scanned back to RGB.

Because it's a model, the controls are physical: camera exposure, print exposure, enlarger filters, how much DIR coupling, grain particle size, halation strength. Push them too far and the image breaks the way film does, with colour crossovers when it's badly over- or underexposed. And you can experimentw with each control. There are about 50 stocks: Portra, Ektar, Gold, Pro 400H, Superia, Kodachrome, Velvia and Provia slide film, Aerochrome and some B&W (HP5, FP4...). There are 9 papers and print films too, such as Endura, Crystal Archive and Vision 2383. The paper choice has a huge impact on the final look.

Negs implements the entire chain and is orders of magnitudes faster than the original python Spektrafilm implementation, so you can play around with sliders and get live feedback.

Feedback is very welcome, especially from people who have actually shot these stocks: tell me which ones look wrong to you.
